rv.q: The emotions this stage biography stirs in theatergoers are genuine, a testament to the bravery and tenacity of the woman whose real-life story is being told.
The conviction of Tovah Feldshuh's transformative performance drives 'Irena's Vow,' but it's the compelling true story of courage and heroism that makes Dan Gordon's by-the-numbers script so moving.
Ms. Opdyke’s potentially moving story is handled in such a banal, ham-fisted manner that it sometimes feels like bad fiction.
With "Irena's Vow," now open on Broadway after a run last fall at Baruch College, the answer's yes.
It's one of the single most dramatic moments in the production, which says an incriminating lot about the flatness of both Gordon's script and Michael Parva's direction.

There is at least one reason to be grateful that Irena's Vow has arrived on Broadway: After this production, it's doubtful that anyone will be itching to produce a stage adaptation of Schindler's List.
